title: Send It Out
theme: The roots mit and miss: sending and letting go
objectives: I can use the root mit/miss (send, let go) to work out the meaning of ten words.
I can explain how a prefix such as sub-, com-, e-, ad-, dis-, or inter- changes the root.
I can choose the right word for handing in work, giving approval, and making a promise.
I can write about a team project using at least four words from this unit.
rationale: Mit and miss are one Latin root with two spellings, so this is students' first look at a root that changes form: mit before most endings, miss before -ion, -ile, and in dismiss. The ten words cover school (submit, dismiss, admit), rules and promises (permit, commit, commission) and science or adventure (emit, missile, mission, intermittent). Each prefix gives a direction of sending: under (sub-), through (per-), with (com-), out (e-), toward (ad-), away (dis-), between (inter-). Students who see that pattern can unlock transmit, remit, omit, and mission-family words in later reading.

words.def: To hand in work or a plan so that others can judge or approve it.
words.ex: Each student must submit the science report by Friday morning.
words.ex2: The robotics club will submit its design to the judges before the contest begins.
words.nonExample: Leaving your essay in your backpack is not the same as submitting it.
words.rel: giving something to people who will judge it

apps.academic: Scientists submit their findings to a journal so that other experts can check them.
apps.spoken: Did you submit the permission form yet?
apps.writing: Use submit when a person hands work or a plan to someone who will judge it.

cloze.s: Mina forgot to ___ her permission slip, so she could not go on the field trip.

cloze2.s: The deadline to ___ entries for the poetry contest is the first of May.

misuse.s: She chose to submit her essay by keeping it hidden in her desk all semester.
misuse.why: To submit is to hand work in; hiding it in a desk is the opposite.

visual.alt: A finished paper being placed in an inbox tray.

words.frame: Before I submit my work, I ___.

words.def: To allow something to happen or to let someone do something.

senses.def: An official paper that says you are allowed to do something.
senses.example: Dad bought a fishing permit before we drove to the lake.

words.ex: The library does not permit food near the computers.
words.ex2: Our camp rules permit each hiker to carry one small snack.
words.nonExample: A sign that says No Entry does not permit anyone to walk through the door.

apps.academic: Laws and school rules state what they permit and what they forbid.
apps.spoken: Our teacher permits us to choose our own partners.
apps.writing: As a verb, permit is stressed on the second syllable; as a noun, on the first.

cloze.s: Our school does not ___ phones during tests, so everyone keeps them in their backpacks.

cloze2.s: The rules ___ each player to bring one guest, but no more than one.

misuse.s: The museum permits photos, so guards stop every visitor who takes one.
misuse.why: To permit is to allow; guards who stop people taking photos are forbidding them.

visual.alt: A green traffic light beside a check mark.

words.frame: My school permits students to ___ but not to ___.

words.def: To promise to do something and stay with it until it is done.
words.ex: Dana decided to commit an hour every night to practicing the cello.
words.ex2: Once the team commits to a plan, everyone has to follow it.
words.nonExample: Saying maybe and walking away is not the same as committing.
words.rel: making a promise and keeping it

apps.academic: Historians ask what a leader was willing to commit to when times got hard.
apps.spoken: I can commit to Saturday, but not to Sunday.
apps.writing: Use commit with to: commit to a plan, a goal, or a team.

cloze.s: Before the season starts, every player must ___ to attending all of the practices.

cloze2.s: Lila wanted to ___ to the hiking club, so she cleared her Saturdays for the whole fall.

misuse.s: Jared committed to the project by quitting after the very first meeting.
misuse.why: To commit is to promise and stay with something; quitting right away is the opposite.

visual.alt: Two people shaking hands above a marked calendar.

words.def: To send out something such as light, sound, heat, or a smell.
words.ex: The old refrigerator emitted a low hum all night long.
words.ex2: Fireflies emit flashes of light that other fireflies can see in the dark.
words.nonExample: A sponge that soaks up water is not emitting it.

morph.note: The prefix e- is a form of ex-, meaning out.

words.rel: sending something out into the air

apps.academic: The sun emits the light and heat that reach Earth.
apps.spoken: That battery is emitting a weird smell.
apps.writing: Use emit for light, sound, heat, or smell that comes out of a source.

cloze.s: The broken smoke alarm began to ___ a loud, steady beep every ten seconds.

cloze2.s: Glow sticks ___ a soft green light after you snap the tube inside them.

misuse.s: The radio emitted loud music, so the room stayed perfectly silent.
misuse.why: Emit means send out; loud music sent out would fill the room, not leave it silent.

visual.alt: A glowing lamp next to a speaker with sound waves.

words.def: To say that something is true, often when you did not want to.

senses.def: To let someone enter a place or join a group.
senses.example: The theater will admit ticket holders at six o'clock.

words.ex: Leo had to admit that his first answer was wrong.
words.ex2: Tara finally admitted that she had left the gate open.
words.nonExample: Blaming someone else for your own mistake is not admitting it.

apps.academic: A good scientist will admit when the data does not support her prediction.
apps.spoken: I have to admit, you were right.
apps.writing: Use admit when a character says aloud something he would rather hide.

cloze.s: After hours of arguing, Ravi had to ___ that he had never read the book.

cloze2.s: A brave leader will ___ a mistake in front of the whole team instead of hiding it.

misuse.s: Jess admitted that she broke the vase by insisting she had never touched it.
misuse.why: To admit is to say the truth; insisting she never touched it is a denial.

visual.alt: A student raising a hand to speak up.

words.frame: It is hard to admit that ___, but I will because ___.

words.def: To tell people they may leave, or to decide not to consider an idea.
words.ex: The teacher dismissed the class five minutes early because of the fire drill.
words.ex2: Do not dismiss Carlos's suggestion until you have heard his whole plan.
words.nonExample: Asking everyone to stay in their seats is not dismissing them.

apps.academic: A judge may dismiss a case when there is not enough evidence to continue.
apps.spoken: Please don't dismiss my idea before I finish explaining it.
apps.writing: Use dismiss for letting a group go, or for waving away an idea.

cloze.s: When the bell rang, the principal ___ the assembly, and the students filed out of the gym.

cloze2.s: It is unfair to ___ a new idea before you have even tried it once.

misuse.s: The principal dismissed the students and told them they must stay in their seats.
misuse.why: Dismissed means told them they may leave; staying in their seats contradicts that.

visual.alt: A school bell above an open classroom door.

words.frame: A teacher dismisses the class when ___.

words.def: An object or weapon that is thrown or launched toward a target.
words.ex: The student's foam missile sailed across the gym and bounced off the target.
words.ex2: At the castle museum, we watched a model catapult hurl a stone missile at a wooden wall.
words.nonExample: A pillow resting on a bed is not a missile.

morph.note: The final e of -ile is kept; the word means something able to be sent.

words.rel: something sent through the air at a target

apps.academic: Physics classes study how the angle of a launch changes how far a missile travels.
apps.spoken: The paper missile hit the wall instead of the trash can.
apps.writing: Missile can mean any launched object, from a foam toy to a weapon, so the context matters.

cloze.s: The foam ___ flew straight at the paper target and knocked it over.

cloze2.s: The toy launcher shoots a soft ___ that bounces harmlessly off the wall.

misuse.s: The missile stayed perfectly still on the table because it had been launched at the target.
misuse.why: A missile that was launched would be moving, not sitting still.

visual.alt: A toy rocket flying toward a bullseye target.

words.frame: A missile needs ___ to reach its target.

words.def: An important task or goal that a person or group is sent or chooses to complete.
words.ex: The astronauts' mission was to repair a panel on the space station.
words.ex2: Our class mission is to clean the creek and count every piece of trash we find.
words.nonExample: Wandering around with no goal in mind is not a mission.
words.rel: an important job someone is sent to do

apps.academic: A mission statement tells what an organization exists to do.
apps.spoken: My mission this weekend is to finish the model.
apps.writing: Use mission when a task matters and a person or team is sent to carry it out.

cloze.s: The rescue team's ___ was to find the lost hikers before dark.

cloze2.s: Our ___ at the food bank is to make sure no neighbor goes hungry.

misuse.s: Our mission is to do nothing at all, so we have no goal to work on.
misuse.why: A mission is an important task or goal; doing nothing is neither.

words.def: Stopping and starting again and again, not steady or continuous.
words.ex: Intermittent rain kept us moving between the picnic shelter and the soccer field.
words.ex2: The radio gave off intermittent static, fading in and out as the car drove through the hills.
words.nonExample: A faucet that runs all day without stopping is not intermittent.

morph.note: The root is spelled mitt in this word.

words.rel: on and off with pauses between

apps.academic: Weather reports use intermittent for showers that come and go during the day.
apps.spoken: My internet has been intermittent all afternoon.
apps.writing: Use intermittent for sounds, lights, or events that keep stopping and starting.

cloze.s: The flashlight gave only ___ light, blinking on and off as the battery wore down.

cloze2.s: Because the Wi-Fi was ___, the video froze every few minutes and then started again.

misuse.s: The intermittent hum from the fan never paused for even one second all night.
misuse.why: Intermittent means stopping and starting; a hum that never pauses is continuous.

visual.alt: A light bulb flickering beside a clock.

words.def: A job or piece of work that someone is formally asked, and often paid, to do.

senses.def: An official group chosen to study a problem or oversee something.
senses.example: The city formed a commission to decide where the new park should go.

words.ex: The painter received a commission to create a mural for the new library.
words.ex2: A local bakery gave Sofia a commission to make a hundred cookies for a wedding.
words.nonExample: A drawing you make just for fun, with no one asking for it, is not a commission.
words.rel: work someone is asked and paid to do

apps.academic: Artists in many periods lived on commissions from wealthy patrons.
apps.spoken: She took a commission to paint our dog's portrait.
apps.writing: Check whether a commission means a paid job or an official group.

cloze.s: The sculptor was thrilled to receive a ___ from the city to design a fountain for the main square.

cloze2.s: Because she needed money for art supplies, Tessa accepted a ___ to paint portraits of three pets.

misuse.s: The artist refused the commission, so she was paid to paint the mural.
misuse.why: A commission is a job someone is asked to do; if she refused it, she would not be paid for it.

visual.alt: A painter working on a large mural on a wall.

words.frame: If I received a commission, I would ___.

passage.title: The Catapult Challenge
paras: Every spring, Mr. Alvarez gave his science class one mission: build a machine that could launch a foam missile across the gym and hit a target eight meters away. Priya's team spent a week drawing plans on graph paper. On Friday they had to submit their design for approval, and Mr. Alvarez circled two problems in red pen.

"I will permit you to test it on Monday," he said, "but only after you fix the arm. It will snap." Omar did not want to hear this. He had built the arm himself, and at first he would not admit that it was too thin. Priya waited until he cooled off. Then she said quietly, "Let's test a thicker one and compare the results."

By Monday the team had agreed to commit every lunch period to testing. The gym's old lights flickered in an intermittent pattern, on for a minute, off for ten seconds, on again. The timer on Jonah's laptop emitted a sharp beep each time the foam missile landed, and he wrote every distance in a table. The first six launches fell short. The seventh landed one meter from the target.

When the bell rang, Mr. Alvarez dismissed the class, but Priya's team stayed to run one more test. Word spread, and the principal stopped by to watch. She liked their careful records so much that the parent group offered the team a commission: build a larger catapult for the spring festival, and the group would pay for the materials plus a small fee.
Omar grinned. "My first arm would have broken in half," he said. "Next time I will listen sooner." Priya laughed. Their mission was only beginning.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "admit" most nearly means
choices: to let someone enter a building
to argue that a plan is perfect
to complain to a teacher
to accept that something is true
qs.why: Omar did not want to say that his arm was too thin, so admit means to say it is true even though he dislikes it.

qs.q: Why does Mr. Alvarez circle two problems on the team's design?
choices: He wants the team to quit the contest.
He thinks the target is too far away.
He plans to build the catapult himself.
He expects the team to fix flaws before testing.
qs.why: He allows testing only after the arm is fixed, so the circled problems are things to repair first.

qs.q: Which detail from paragraph 3 best shows that the lights were intermittent?
choices: The gym was old.
They were on for a minute, off for ten seconds, and on again.
The timer emitted a sharp beep.
The seventh launch landed one meter from the target.
qs.why: Intermittent means stopping and starting, and the on-off pattern is the detail that shows it.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, what does the parent group's commission ask the team to do?
choices: Do a paid building job for the festival
Join the parent group as members
Throw away the first catapult
Test the old catapult in the lunchroom
qs.why: The group asks for a larger catapult and will pay for materials plus a fee, so commission means a paid job.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Foam missiles are the best way to learn science.
Teams succeed when members admit flaws and keep testing.
Principals should judge every science project.
Thin materials always break in a catapult.
qs.why: Omar accepts the problem with his arm, the team keeps testing, and the results improve.

write.prompt: Describe a project you worked on with others. Use at least four words from this unit to explain what you had to submit, what you had to commit to, and what went wrong or right.
write.frame: Our mission was to ___, so we had to commit to ___ and submit ___.

study.task: Pick three words from the unit that share the root mit or miss. For each, name the prefix, say what the prefix adds to the idea of sending, and write a sentence that shows the meaning. Then explain when the root is spelled mit and when it is spelled miss.

groups.label: letting people or things in, out, or away
things that are sent and pauses in a signal

choices: give : receive
loud : noisy
pen : write
bird : wing
ball : throw
hot : cold
teacher : school
quick : fast
analogies.relation: an object and the action used to send it

sentences: Write a sentence about something a school should permit and something it should not. Explain why in the same sentence.
Write a sentence that uses both commit and mission about a team you know.
Write a sentence about a time you had to admit you were wrong. Say what you admitted.
Write a sentence using intermittent to describe a sound or light you noticed this week.

given: Maya wanted to enter the contest.
She had to submit her drawing by noon.
combine.model: Maya had to submit her drawing by noon if she wanted to enter the contest.

given: The lamp gave off a faint glow.
combine.model: During the blackout, the lamp emitted an intermittent glow that came and went all evening.

discuss: What is the difference between a person who commits to a plan and a person who only says yes? Use commit in your answer.
Should a school permit students to use phones at lunch? Use permit and one reason.
When is it better to dismiss an idea, and when is it a mistake? Explain.
produce.explain: Explain how the prefix changes the meaning in emit and admit. Use the idea of sending to show why e- and ad- give different directions.

argue.prompt: Claim: Students should be allowed to resubmit a project after getting feedback. Take a side and support it with two reasons, using words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. A student who can resubmit might ___.

constructed.prompt: Your class is entering a poster contest. Write two sentences that explain the rules, using submit and permit.
look: states a clear rule for each word
keeps the sentences in the context of a contest
constructed.model: Each student must submit one poster by Friday. The rules permit teams of two, but they do not permit posters that are copied from the internet.

constructed.prompt: A character makes a mistake on a group project. Write what the character admits and what the character commits to doing next.
constructed.model: Eli admitted that he had forgotten to print the charts. He committed to arriving early the next morning and printing every page himself.

constructed.prompt: Write a short description of a school fire drill or storm that uses dismiss, intermittent, and emit.
look: shows each word with a sensory or action detail
constructed.model: The alarm emitted a piercing sound, and intermittent flashes of light bounced off the hall. When the drill ended, the principal dismissed every class.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words built on the Latin root mit/miss (send, let go) and see how seven prefixes change its direction. They meet the root in a team-project narrative, practice the mit-to-miss spelling shift, and use the words in sentences, a discussion, and a short argument about resubmitting work.

notes.va.submit.v: Build the word from parts on the board: sub- (under) + mit (send). Show that submit means to hand work over to someone who will judge it. Note that submit also has a second meaning, to give in to a stronger force, which the passage does not use.
notes.va.permit.v: Stress changes with part of speech: per-MIT (verb) and PER-mit (noun). Have students say the sentence 'I need a permit, and the park will permit me to fish' aloud. Contrast with forbid on the shades ladder.
notes.va.commit.v: Commit to a plan is the taught use. Students sometimes know only commit a crime; acknowledge it as a different use and keep the focus on promising and staying with something. Ask what a person does to show they have committed.
notes.va.emit.v: Emit is for things coming out of a source: light, sound, heat, smell. Contrast with absorb. Ask students to name three emitters in the room (a lamp, a speaker, a heater).
notes.va.admit.v: Teach the confession sense first and name the second sense, to let someone in, as a different use. Students often confuse admit with accept; admit is about saying a truth, not receiving a gift. Practice with a two-line role-play.
notes.va.dismiss.v: Dismiss has a people sense (let them go) and an idea sense (refuse to consider). Link the dis- (away) to both. Be prepared for students to think dismissal always means punishment.
notes.va.missile.n: Define as any launched object and let context set the tone, since students will think first of weapons. Tie to the passage's foam missile and to the study of projectile motion in science.
notes.va.mission.n: Miss + -ion: the act or result of being sent. Contrast with goal: a mission is a task someone is sent or chooses to complete. Ask what the mission of your classroom is.
notes.va.intermittent.adj: Model the spelling mitt and the parts: inter- (between) + mitt (send, let go) + -ent. Draw a pulse line to show on-off-on. Contrast with continuous.
notes.va.commission.n: Two uses: a paid job (taught) and an official group (second sense). Show both in sentences and ask which fits an artist and which fits a city. Students may confuse it with mission because both come from miss.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I see the word dismiss. The prefix dis- means away, and miss is the root that means send or let go. So dismiss is to send away. In the passage, Mr. Alvarez dismissed the class, so he told them they could leave. That matches the root and the prefix.'
discuss: Which mit/miss word would you most like to see on a report card, and why?
How does knowing one root help you guess the meaning of a word you have never seen?
misconceptions: Emit and omit are the same word.
Admit only means to let someone in.
Commission and mission have the same meaning.
A missile is always a weapon.
extend: Find three more words in a dictionary that contain mit or miss and sort them by prefix.
Write a short scene in which a character must submit something and then admit a mistake.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the mit-to-miss spelling pattern two days later with a quick sort of the ten words, then at one week as an oral round of 'send it out'. Connect suspend, dispense, and compute from earlier units as other roots that carry a clear core meaning.

frames: The teacher will permit us to ___ if ___.
I had to admit that ___, so I committed to ___.
wida.oral: Partner A acts out one word without speaking (for example, handing in a paper). Partner B names the unit word and says which prefix and which root build it.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: presentar (submit), comprometerse (commit), despedir; descartar (dismiss), encargo (commission), misil; proyectil (missile). Admitir for admit may be less natural than reconocer in some regions.

Sense boundaries: submit (also 'give in to authority', not taught), commit (also 'commit a crime', named in teacher note only), dismiss (people and idea uses combined in one definition), commission (paid job taught; official group as second sense).
Root meaning 'send; let go' for mit/miss is stated without an origin claim beyond the glossed meaning; missile segments (miss + -ile, 'able to be sent') are a teaching gloss, not a historical claim.
